title: Words for a massacre
hook: a tiger among the sheep: in Asa, Guru Nanak's hymn on the invasion asks the Master of the flock to answer for the ordinary people who suffered

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Patti, an alphabet set in a raga and signed by Nanak the poet. Your line was the alphabet sings. Did your letter's line carry itself through the day? Today the songs turn heavy. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-nine.

Two heavyweights step into a ring. Both trained, both chose to be there, and when one goes down, the crowd groans but nobody calls it a crime. Now change the scene. A tiger comes down a hillside into a field of sheep. Nobody chose this fight. The sheep can't hit back. The two scenes are not the same thing. Guru Nanak sang exactly that difference, about an invasion of Punjab, in a hymn in Raga Asa on ang three sixty. Sikhs call his hymns on that invasion the Babarvani.
screen: `TWO FIGHTERS IN A RING.` → `A TIGER AMONG THE SHEEP.` → `THE BABARVANI.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Babarvani puts the name of Babur, the invader, beside vani, words. A small group of hymns by Guru Nanak, about what Babur's armies did. One of those hymns even uses the phrase itself for the invader's sway: Babar vaanee spread. Second, the hymn on ang three sixty, in paraphrase. Khurasan is taken under the invader's hand, and Hindustan is put in terror. Then the hymn's center, the Rahao, turns to God, in paraphrase: Creator, you are the Master of all. If the powerful strike the powerful, the mind holds no grievance. And the next verse holds the ring and the field together: but if a powerful tiger falls on a flock, the Master of the flock must answer for it. That's the whole moral picture, in one image. Guru Nanak doesn't grieve for kings losing to kings. He grieves for the flock: farmers, families, people who never chose a side and couldn't fight back. Third, notice where he takes that grief. Not to the invader, not to a crowd. To God, as the Master who is answerable. Earlier on this path we heard this hymn's cry, did you feel no pain? Today, hear the logic under it. If God is Master of all, then the flock is God's flock, and its suffering is not a footnote. It is the point. Fourth, the hymn says the jewel of the land was spoiled, and no one cared for the dead. Guru Nanak names the cost in ordinary lives. These are words for a massacre, kept in scripture and still sung, so that the ones without power are remembered in the Guru's own voice. Today's line: he named the pain.
screen: `BABARVANI: WORDS ON BABUR'S INVASION.` · `THE RING AND THE FLOCK.` · `THE MASTER MUST ANSWER.` · `THE COST IN ORDINARY LIVES.` · then, large: `HE NAMED THE PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold those caught in war. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people living through war today, not the leaders or the armies, but the flock: a family packing in a hurry, a child at a shelter, an old man who won't leave his house. You don't need names or places. If you pray, you can pray for them in the way your own tradition prays, or say Waheguru on each breath out. If you don't pray, keep them in mind with each breath, as if you were sitting beside them. The bell holds the time.
Babarvani. Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion, which grieve for the flock, not the kings, and bring that grief to the Master of all. Today's word.
Your line: he named the pain. Today, when you meet news of war, find one ordinary person in the story, and say their situation to yourself in plain words. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: The Babarvani hymns are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib like any other Gurbani; some Sikhs turn to them when remembering victims of violence and speaking about justice for ordinary people.

fork.setup: the hymn sets two kinds of violence side by side. which one does it say the Master of the flock must answer for?
options: a powerful tiger falling on a flock.
fork.reveal: if the powerful strike the powerful, the mind holds no grievance. but if a tiger falls on a flock, the Master must answer for it.

original.note: khasmai: to the Master, the owner of the flock; the hymn says the Master must answer for it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn about an invasion is about who won.
what it means: it grieves for the flock, ordinary people who never chose the fight, and asks God to answer.
what a scholar hears: the Rahao, kartaa toon sabhnaa kaa soee, then the tiger and the flock: khasmai saa pursaaee, the Master is answerable.

sources.ref: Asa, Mahala 1, 'khuraasaan khasmaanaa keeaa hindusataan daraaiaa', Ang 360

notes: Ang 360 hymn paraphrased: Khurasan spared (khasmaanaa keeaa) and Hindustan terrified; Rahao 'kartaa toon sabhnaa kaa soee, je sakataa sakate kau maare taa man ros na hoee'; 'sakataa seehu maare pai vagai khasmai saa pursaaee'; 'ratan vigaarr vigoe kutee muiaa saar na kaaee'. 'Mind feels no grief' renders ros (anger, resentment); please confirm. The 'dogs' of the last line are not voiced.
'Khurasan was spared' renders khasmaanaa keeaa (took Khurasan under his ownership/protection); commentators differ; please confirm.

The name Babarvani is glossed as Babur's name beside vani; the teach also says one hymn uses the phrase 'baabar vaanee' (Ang 417, 'jadahu baabar vaanee fir gaee'). Please confirm the line and that 'sway' fairly renders vaanee there.
'A small group of hymns' is used instead of a count; traditionally four hymns (Ang 360, 417–418, 722–723). Confirm whether to state the count.
Earlier days (40, 979) used this hymn's 'did you feel no pain' line; this day takes the tiger-and-flock Rahao as its new angle.
Babur's faith and the Mughal name are not stated, to avoid making any community a foil.
Original: ਖਸਮੈ and pronunciation; please confirm.

Editor pass: the tiger-and-flock line is no longer attributed to the Rahao (it is the verse after it); 'Khurasan was spared' replaced with a neutral rendering of 'khasmaanaa keeaa'; ros rendered 'grievance' rather than 'grief' in voice and games; howItsDone's 'often' softened to 'some'.
